title: Models and Experiments
text:
Why read science?

Traditionally, scientific knowledge is shared through written documents.
We read science to

identify and verify knowledge that can be used in professional work and decision-making
identify and verify techniques and methods that we can use; develop new questions based on the findings of the authors
be entertained and feed our curiousity




mention that this lab presentation re-iterates some of the content that will be included in lecture module 2; mention that we’ll be talking about different types of scientific documents in lecture module 3; mention that we’ll be working through creating some written documents throughout this course
highlight that the subpoints are linking to “Information Gathering”, “Finding Inspiration” and “Being entertainment/a sense of wonder” from lecture module 2

title: Models and Experiments
text:
Why is reading science hard?

Everything is new to the reader
Everything is new to the author
Everything moves quickly / People don’t have a lot of time


Taking your time and learning how to read science is a super power!



explain that usually, as a reader, you are reading papers or technical notes or even books in a research area that you are new to. so you may not be familiar with some of the concepts, foundational theories, or even writing practices of the field (some areas have “predictable” syntax, notation, etc.)
explain a subtle but important fact–many scientific publications are the first time the author is explaning something (especially true for journal articles). Authors might understand their results perfectly, but still are figuring out best ways to share the ideas.
explain these two challenges are linked to a societal challenge: science and life appear to move quickly. Authors do not take as much time to think about what they want to share, they may not edit as carefully as they like. Readers don’t have the time to learn foundations of a research area, don’t try very hard to engage if they don’t understand the article the first-time they read it
emphasize that building quality reading skills takes time and practice.. it’s more than just reading the words, its trying to appreciate and understand what the author is trying to say. Also emphasize that being “slow” now as a student is a good thing–better to be slow now and learn the skills well

title: Models and Experiments
text:
Building a reading strategy

getting better at reading takes time and requires practice
it also helps to have a strategy
Choose the elements of your strategy:

content: what do you want to get better at reading?
frequency: how often are you going to read?
tracking: how are you going to track your reading/progress?
community: who will you talk about your readings with?

title: Reading and Note-taking
text:
Tracking your reading

a reading log is a document/tool that scientists use to keep track of their reading

can be a physical document you edit by hand
can be a digital document you edit on a computer/phone
can be embedded within a software tool




note that logs are tools not just for scientists–other researchers, writers, marketters, etc.

explain that the “log” can take any form (a note on your phone to a dedicated spreadsheet)

title: Reading and Note-taking
text:
Tracking your reading

an annotated bibliography extends the idea of a reading log to include key information about the materials being read

having a well-formatted annotated bibliography can be incredibly useful as a scientist




this key information could include author information, summary of the material, an appraisal/critical evaluation, etc.
especially useful when trying to design experiments, remember facts and figures, write papers, etc.
make a note that it is common for scientst to build an annotated bibliography as the first step when they are starting a new research project

title: Reading and Note-taking
text:
Building an annotated bibliography

there are seemingly infinite ways to construct an annotated bibliography; the most important quality of an annotated bibliography is that it is useful to the user(s)
in this class, we’ll use a template annotated bibliography developed by Arun



explain that if you can’t pull the information you need to help you with the project you are working on, then your annotated bibliography is not well constructed
note that the template includes questions to help guide reading/thinking about the material

title: Reading and Note-taking
text:
Identifying papers

we cannot “identify” papers by only title
we cannot “identify” papers by only author(s)
we cannot “identify” papers by only journal
we “identify” papers by full citation
we “identify” papers by Digital Object Identifier (DOI)



there can be more than one paper with the same title
most authors publish multiple papers
journals publish so many papers
you can often uniquely identify a paper by author + title (rare that an author will publish two different papers with the same title)
you can often uniquely identify a paper by author + title + year (even more rare that an author will publish two papers with the same title in the same year)
the best way to be sure you are uniquely identifying a paper is the full citation (authors, title, year, journal, volume, issue, pages, etc.)
the best way in modern times is to use a digital object identifier (DOI); every paper published paper since 1997 (28 years ago) has been assigned a DOI–it’s a persistent identifier and will be fixed for the lifetime of the paper.
In our class, we’ll often be assigning papers by their DOI.. you can enter a DOI into google scholar and very quickly identify the paper
You can also use OMNI (if want to avoid google search limitations) as will be discussed in Lecture Module 3

title: Reading and Note-taking
text:
Learning a reference manager

a reference manager is a software tool to help you organize your readings
many modern reference managers allow you to:

upload and annotate your pdfs
sync your library across multiple computers
include searchable tags
interface with word processors to automate citations and bibliography creation

it will be incredibly advantageous to become comfortable with a reference manager



make a note of several of the popular open-source and commercially available references managers: mendeley, endnote, refworks,… new references managers everyday

title: Reading and Note-taking
text:
Zotero

a popular open-source reference manager that is supported at Trent University:

https://www.zotero.org/

you can create a free account so you can sync Zotero across multiple device
you can download and use Zotero without an accout (on a single machine)
you can install the MS-Word plug-in to integrate Zotero with the desktop version of Word



note that it is Arun’s favourite reference manager, and staff in the Library and through Academic Skills should be able to assist students with Zotero issues
also note that they have paid tiers of zotero accounts with increased storage and other features–might be handy if you end up reading a lot of papers
provide a live demo of (5-10 minutes) Zotero. The key things to showcase:

adding a file to a zotero library
opening the paper so you can annotate it
creating searchable tags
adding a reference by just citation
adding a manual entry link to a youtube video (as an example)
generating a bibliography in a specified format
linking to word, adding citations, adding a bibliography

reordering sentences, updating bibliography, changing bibliography format

title: Research Dissemination
text:
Why read science?

Traditionally, scientific knowledge is shared through written documents.
We read science to

identify and verify knowledge that can be used in professional work and decision-making
identify and verify techniques and methods that we can use; develop new questions based on the findings of the authors
be entertained and feed our curiousity




mention that this lab presentation re-iterates some of the content that will be included in lecture module 2; mention that we’ll be talking about different types of scientific documents in lecture module 3; mention that we’ll be working through creating some written documents throughout this course

title: Research Dissemination
text:
Why is reading science hard?

Everything is new to the reader
Everything is new to the author
Everything moves quickly / People don’t have a lot of time


Taking your time and learning how to read science is a super power!



explain that usually, as a reader, you are reading papers or technical notes or even books in a research area that you are new to. so you may not be familiar with some of the concepts, foundational theories, or even writing practices of the field (some areas have “predictable” syntax, notation, etc.)
explain a subtle but important fact–many scientific publications are the first time the author is explaning something (especially true for journal articles). Authors might understand their results perfectly, but still are figuring out best ways to share the ideas.
explain these two challenges are linked to a societal challenge: science and life appear to move quickly. Authors do not take as much time to think about what they want to share, they may not edit as carefully as they like. Readers don’t have the time to learn foundations of a research area, don’t try very hard to engage if they don’t understand the article the first-time they read it
emphasize that building quality reading skills takes time and practice.. it’s more than just reading the words, its trying to appreciate and understand what the author is trying to say. Also emphasize that being “slow” now as a student is a good thing–better to be slow now and learn the skills well

content: what do you want to get better at reading?
frequency: how often are you going to read?
tracking: how are you going to track your reading/progress?
community: who will you talk about your readings with?

FRSC 2020H is an undergraduate course in the FRSC program, that:

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
On Epistemology

a branch of philosophy interested in the origin, nature and limits of human knowledge
Some ways we think we know:

Personal experience
Authority
Tradition
Intuition
Reasoning
Observation/evidence




how do we know things? why do we believe things?
But all these individual methods of knowing are fallible

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
What is science?

a knowledge base constructed using the “scientific method”
the scientific method is (an iterative) process for learning about anything, and can be summarized by the following general steps:

observing
recognizing/defining
hypothesizing
testing
(disseminating)




many bodies of knowledge are described as “science” or “a science” and they are similar in that the knowledge was acquired by following the so-called “scientific method”

observing: to notice or perceive something (of interest) in a situation
recognizing/defining: using observations to recognize open questions or define problems
hypothesizing: using observations and other available information to infer solutions to the questions/problems
testing: designing models and/or experiments to evaluate hypotheses and predictions

(disseminating): sharing results so others can make observations, and build knowledge


the key to what’s the scientific method so effective is that we allow iteration, we allow for ideas to grow and change as new information becomes available–science is dynamic knowledge
the verb to iterate means to cycle/repeat through a process, but leverage information learned through previous iterations (passes through the method)

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
History of scientific development (1/5)

Approximately 1600 BCE - Edwin Smith Papyrus

Describes 48 battlefield injuries and the surgical treatments employed, considered to be the world’s earliest known medical document and contains essential elements of the scientific method
Purchased in 1862 by egyptologist Edwin Smith




the scientific method didn’t just get written down as a fully formed idea, it itself developed over time–through iteration

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
History of scientific development (2/5)

4th Century BCE - Greek Philosophy

Deductive Reasoning: A form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from accepted premises
Top-Down reasoning
Susceptible to failure if any of the premises are incorrect

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
History of scientific development (3/5)

4th Century BCE- Greek Philosophy

Inductive Reasoning: A form of reasoning in which an inference (hypothesis) is generated based on observations
Bottom-up reasoning
Always inconclusive, but can be used to generate theory, hypotheses, and probabilistic statements

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
History of scientific development (4/5)

8th-15th century CE - Islamic Science; 12th-16th century CE European Science

Extend deductive-inductive reasoning with controlled experimentation (empiricism)
Increased emphasis on mathematics to formulate and describe theory
Introduced principle of parsimony: An explanation or theory should be as simple as possible and contain just enough terms to explain the facts. (Ockham’s Razor)

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
History of scientific development (5/5)

16th - 18th century CE - Scientific Revolution

1543 - Copernicus published “On the revolutions of the heavenly spheres”” proposed that the earth is not center-point of the universe
1655 - Hook published “Micrographia”; described observations under a microscope
By the end of the 18th century, the scientific method (iterative inductive-deducting reasoning with well-designed experiments) was widely regarded as the best strategy for acquiring knowledge (learning)

title: Course Preliminaries
section: Modern thoughts on the scientific method
text:
Modern thoughts on the scientific method

In 1934, Karl Popper introduced the concept of “falsifiabilty” to determine whether a statement (e.g., a hypothesis or theory) was scientific:

a statement is considered scientific if it can be falsified (refuted) using an empirical test

At present, most people agree that the scientific method is the reliable approach to learning, but many people are challenging the way it is taught

Windschitl et al. Beyond the scientific method: Model-based inquiry as a paradigm of preference for school science investigations. Science Education, 92(5), 941-967.

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
Good Science is…

Empirical.
Rational.
Testable.
Parsimonious.
Explainable.
Reliable.
Tentative.


Empirical: based on observations or experience
Rational: consistent with reason or logic
Testable: able to be tested
Parsimonious: does not make many assumptions
Explainable: able to be explained
Reliable: able to be trusted
Tentative: not certain of fixed; provisional

title: Course Preliminaries
section: Basic application of the scientific method (1/2)
text:
Basic application of the scientific method (1/2)

Situation: You are working as a forensic chemist in a drug lab. You are asked to evaluate a baggie that contains an unidentified white powder.
Observation: The baggie is a standard size for illegal recreational drugs, and the visual consistency of the powder is similar to cocaine.

title: Course Preliminaries
section: Basic application of the scientific method (2/2)
text:
Basic application of the scientific method (2/2)

Hypothesis: The substance in the baggie is cocaine.
Test: We can use lab techniques (analytical chemistry) to determine whether sample is cocaine. We take a sample of the material to the lab.
Results: The lab results suggest that the sample is not cocaine.
Follow up questions: …



is it another illegal recreational drug?
did you take enough sample?
what was the lab technique used?
was the analytical instrument working correctly?
there is a danger of trying too hard to make your test meet your expectations–one of the biggest abuses of scientific method is tweaking.

title: Course Preliminaries
section: The scientific method in forensic science
text:
The scientific method in forensic science

Forensic science has unique challenges:

Usually we’re investigating something bad: crime, accident, catastrophic event; hard not form a bias
We only have access to limited information; there’s a lot of uncertainty
Being wrong can have significant consequences; we want to minimize errors
We’re communicating findings to a non-technical audience; there are opportunities for misunderstanding

Important that we use systematic (and validated) approaches to minimize these challenges

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
Some terms to know (1/4)

Information: a description or statement or other form of expression
Fact: information that has been verified as true
Knowledge: the collection of facts and information known by an individual

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
Some terms to know (2/4)

Observing: to notice or perceive something (of interest) in a situation
Hypothesis: a potential answer to a question/problem; not assumed to be true
Falsifiability: the ability of a statement to be proven false; a required property of a scientific hypothesis
Inference: a statement based on the evaluation of available data or evidence; usually stated with some uncertainty

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
Some terms to know (3/4)

Experiment: a procedure for collecting observations, testing a hypothesis, or demonstrating a fact
Deductive reasoning: a form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn logically from accepted premises
Inductive reasoning: a form of reasoning in which an inference (hypothesis) is generated based on observation

title: Course Preliminaries
text:
Some terms to know (4/4)

Iterative process: a cyclical process where each cycle is informed by the previous cycles (also known as iterations)
Hypothetico-deductive reasoning: an alternative description of the iterative inductive-deductive reasoning cycle that is core to the scientific method

Taking your time and learning how to read science is a super power!



explain that usually, as a reader, you are reading papers or technical notes or even books in a research area that you are new to. so you may not be familiar with some of the concepts, foundational theories, or even writing practices of the field (some areas have “predictable” syntax, notation, etc.)
explain a subtle but important fact–many scientific publications are the first time the author is explaning something (especially true for journal articles). Authors might understand their results perfectly, but still are figuring out best ways to share the ideas.
explain these two challenges are linked to a societal challenge: science and life appear to move quickly. Authors do not take as much time to think about what they want to share, they may not edit as carefully as they like. Readers don’t have the time to learn foundations of a research area, don’t try very hard to engage if they don’t understand the article the first-time they read it
emphasize that building quality reading skills takes time and practice.. it’s more than just reading the words, its trying to appreciate and understand what the author is trying to say. Also emphasize that being “slow” now as a student is a good thing–better to be slow now and learn the skills well

getting better at reading takes time and requires practice
it also helps to have a strategy
Choose the elements of your strategy:

content: what do you want to get better at reading?
frequency: how often are you going to read?
tracking: how are you going to track your reading/progress?
community: who will you talk about your readings with?

title: Critical thinking and data analysis
text:
Why read science?

Traditionally, scientific knowledge is shared through written documents.
We read science to

identify and verify knowledge that can be used in professional work and decision-making
identify and verify techniques and methods that we can use; develop new questions based on the findings of the authors
be entertained and feed our curiousity




mention that this lab presentation re-iterates some of the content that will be included in lecture module 2; mention that we’ll be talking about different types of scientific documents in lecture module 3; mention that we’ll be working through creating some written documents throughout this course
highlight that the subpoints are linking to “Information Gathering”, “Finding Inspiration” and “Being entertainment/a sense of wonder” from lecture module 2
